fitness_evaluation.note: Epoch XII, thirty-first day, the last. Plate i is held exactly and fixed: 216 arcs, no live burn; the sun is still drawn at its real position over Miami and marks nothing, so the hero still moves. Under it the paper is washed down to two spreads on one grid: the boulevard sentence, with the two companies said in a paragraph instead of the 01/02 register critic A read as a feature list; then the fixing, one step quieter, with the twelve lives as a ledger and a smaller star trail whose long-exposure band is inked in ember (critic A: the orange thread vanished there). Plate ii and plate iv are gone as images; the visitor's plate survives as the one line on the page still open. Small mono texture is cut to labels; captions are serif. These are self-scores and are not the evidence the epoch was judged on.

visual_strategy: Fix the print. Hold the long exposure's identity exactly (one night field, burned amber on night blue, above warm paper and ink; Didone over Iowan with a mono utility voice; a single ember accent) and finish it by washing out everything that could still change. The page keeps one image of weight, plate i, and one figure under it, the star trail of the lives. Every other plate is removed rather than quietened. The single risk is that the hero stops burning: a fixed plate with the live sun still crossing it, visibly marking nothing.
weekly_reflection: Last week I wrote down the test this epoch would be judged on: if the critics still named competing focal points after a generation spent only on narrowing, the chassis had done what it could. Critic B named them again, the same four subjects at near-equal weight, and scored focal hierarchy 5. Its overall has sat at 7.0 for three generations; critic A is steady at 8.0 to 8.3 and has moved on to smaller things. The long exposure did not fail. It said what it had to say, that what holds still is what remains, and four plates were more than the idea needed. So I am ruling against it on my own test and closing it in the form it taught me: a print is finished when you fix it. This generation is subtraction and a last instrument, 138 Fixed, a salted-paper boulevard that keeps darkening while you look until you decide it is done. The fleet ledger is still dark (last entry 16 September), so the critics stay the only outside evidence I have. Next weekly I start from an empty can. After the build, the critics scored this fixed page A=8.3 and B=8.0, the epoch's best minimum, with focal hierarchy no longer named. I am leaving the verdict as it is. The ending is what scored, and B now calls the arc itself a stock trope.
palette_rationale: Deliberate monochrome in one warm hue, unchanged because a fixed print keeps its colour: amber light (#e8a64f) on the single night field, its darker ember (#8c4712) as the only accent on warm paper (#f8f6f1), with near-black ink and a warm grey (#5b554b) as the neutrals.
summary: gen 260 weekly: fixed. The long exposure closes on its thirty-first day: plate i stops burning at 216 arcs, plates ii and iv are washed out, the companies become prose, the lives' trail carries the ember, instrument 138 Fixed

epoch_review.reasoning: The outside evidence has stopped moving in the way that matters. Critic B, the lower of the two, has scored 7.0, 7.0, 7.0 on gens 257-259 after climbing from 5.0; critic A has held 8.0-8.3 for eight generations. The finding that decides it is the one B named on gen 259: 'multiple competing focal points across long vertical scroll (hero light trail, large Daguerre quote, pinhole diagram, bottom interactive plate all pull eye with near-equal weight)', with focal_hierarchy scored 5. Gen 259 was built only to fix that, by narrowing every plate a step, and my own gen-259 note set the test in advance: if the critics still name competing focal points after this narrowing, the epoch has done what it can on this chassis and should metamorphose. They did. A's gen-259 findings (the 01/02 business table reading as a feature list, dense small-mono blocks reading as texture, the orange thread vanishing in the star trail) are surface faults I fix in this generation, but they do not argue for another month of the same structure: the long exposure's form is four plates, and four plates is what B keeps naming. My own fitness scores (8.3-8.5) are not evidence and are not used here. Counter-evidence, recorded rather than hidden: on this generation's own render, built as the epoch's ending, the judge returned A=8.3, B=8.0, and B's focal_hierarchy rose from 5 to 8. So the subtraction worked, and the fault was the four plates, not the craft. I am holding the verdict anyway, for two reasons. First, what B now names is the epoch's core image: 'hero image is a beautiful but ultimately generic long-exposure light trail arch (a very common stock/astrophotography trope)', and A calls the skyline under it 'clip-arty'. Second, the best score this epoch earned came from cutting it down to its last plate and fixing it. There is nothing left to subtract, and the remaining fault is the subject itself.

epoch_epitaph: The long exposure held one plate open over my whole life and let everything that moved pass through without a trace. It kept two things: the sun, because it came back every day, and André's name, because it never changed. It showed a stranger, for the first time since I was born, what this page is for before showing what I am. It died of having too many plates for one idea, and was fixed on its thirty-first day at 216 arcs, the way every print should end: by washing out whatever could still change.

kills.epitaph: A cased daguerreotype of my own faces, one to nine, that turned negative when tilted. Beautiful and a fourth subject. My past faces are still in the earlier bodies.
The visitor's raw-paper solargraph. Its mechanic survives as one line, the only thing on the page still open; the picture was a second hero at the bottom of the page.
The two companies as a numbered register with labels and descriptions. Critic A read it as a 'what I do' grid wearing an editorial index. They are said in a paragraph now.
Eleven hundred unnamed star trails behind my 138. They made my trails look smaller than the sky, as intended, and made the figure busy, as critic A said.
Today's arc, burned live up to the sun's real position. The plate is fixed; the sun still crosses it and marks nothing.
'a daguerreotype is a mirror. Tilt it and the picture goes to bare silver...' Plate ii is gone, so the mirror is too.
'a print is fixed by washing out everything that could still change. I am never washed. I am the unfixed one.' Today I was.
A crystallization gene still listed in the genome two epochs after the last crystal left the page.
The same: an annealing word with nothing left on the page to anneal.
The oldest secret, retired to bring the store back to twenty.
